status: DRAFT — reviewed by Legal Lead 2026-10-10 against the City's Oct 9, 2026 draft amendments table (pp. 5, 11–13, 17, 19, 38–44, 47), the City CAO webpage, WWMC 20.212, the Facet July 1, 2026 memo, and the PC Sept 14 minutes. Attorney review (Hayner) still required before ATTORNEY-REVIEWED. Every number traces to research/FACTS.md.
disclaimer: This map is a community awareness tool, not an official determination. Stream lines and the 100-foot band come from the City of Walla Walla's own public GIS layers (published Oct 6, 2026), measured from stream centerlines. The proposed ordinance measures buffers from the ordinary high water mark, top of bank, or channel migration zone, whichever is greater, so the regulated area may be larger than shown. Only the City can determine whether a specific property is subject to critical-areas rules. Nothing here is legal advice. Confirm with City of Walla Walla Development Services (509-524-4710, permits@wallawallawa.gov) or a land-use attorney before you buy, sell, build, or decide anything about your property.

inside.headline: This point is inside the proposed 100-foot stream buffer as mapped.
inside.summary: Under the draft Critical Areas Ordinance before City Council (hearing Oct 14, vote scheduled Oct 28, 2026), the minimum buffer on every named creek in the city goes from 35 feet (50 on Yellowhawk) to 100 feet, plus a new 15-foot building setback beyond the buffer, up from 5 feet. Inside the band, the draft's general rule is that all structures and activities must be located outside the buffer unless an exception applies. Existing homes stay; the rules bite when you build, expand, or rebuild.

items.a: Yes. Legally built homes and structures continue as nonconforming structures under city code chapter 20.212, which the draft leaves in place. Nothing requires you to move, remove, or plant anything on day one. The new rules apply when you apply for a permit to build, expand, or rebuild. If adopted Oct 28, the ordinance takes effect Dec 31, 2026.

items.q: Can I repair or maintain what I have?
items.a: Yes. The draft allows maintenance and repair of existing buildings, fences, roads and utilities as long as the work does not encroach further into the buffer, and lets you keep mowing, weeding, pruning, gardening, and maintaining pathways and patios as they existed before adoption. Fences can be replaced or newly built.

items.q: Can I add on, or build a shop, shed, ADU, or new patio inside the band?
items.a: The draft says new structures must be outside the buffer and the 15-foot setback, and it has no rule for additions to homes already inside the band. Existing city code (20.212) lets a nonconforming building extend along its existing line but not closer to the stream. Whether a landward addition or ADU on a house inside the band will be allowed, or will need a critical-areas report and a buffer reduction (averaging stops at 75 feet at its narrowest point on a 100-foot buffer, and the Oct 9 draft deletes the old reduction-with-planting option; a separate rule lets the director exclude buffer areas cut off by pavement or buildings) or a reasonable-use exception, has not been answered in writing. A new patio or uncovered deck is allowed in the 15-foot setback but not in the buffer.

items.q: If my house burns down, can I rebuild?
items.a: Yes, if you apply within six months. The draft itself is silent and defers to existing city code 20.212, which says a damaged nonconforming structure loses its grandfathered status unless a building-permit application to repair or rebuild is filed within six months of the damage. Under that same existing code, reconstruction costing more than 25% of replacement value also needs a conditional-use permit. Miss the six-month window and the structure loses its grandfathered status, so a rebuild would have to meet the new 100-foot buffer and setback. The draft adds no fix, although residents and a commissioner asked for one at the Sept 14 hearing.

items.q: Can I remove trees or clear brush inside the band?
items.a: Noxious weeds and invasive species can be removed by hand or light equipment, and hazard trees with a certified arborist's input. A lawn that existed before adoption can keep being mowed. Other clearing and grading inside the buffer needs authorization, and the draft lists 'restore degraded parts of the buffer' as a measure the City can require when you apply for a permit.

items.q: Can I subdivide or build on a vacant lot with a creek?
items.a: Only the land outside the 100-foot buffer plus the 15-foot setback counts: 115 feet from the high-water mark before a wall can go up. On a 9,600 sq ft lot (about 100 by 100 feet), a creek along one edge can leave no buildable area. The outs are buffer averaging (narrowest point at least 75 feet), a ruling that part of the buffer is cut off by existing pavement or buildings, or a reasonable-use exception, which the draft defines as applying only where the code 'would deny all reasonable use of the property.'

items.q: Will this change my property value or assessment?
items.a: Nobody knows. The City has published no economic, parcel-count, or housing-capacity analysis of the change, and the County Assessor has taken no position. Buildable area affects value; ask the Assessor rather than assuming either direction.

items.q: What does it cost to find out whether I can build?
items.a: Any permit near a creek needs a critical-areas report by a qualified professional (the City says a property owner 'typically needs to hire a biologist') to locate the ordinary high water mark and assess the buffer. The draft makes reports valid for five years. The cost is not stated anywhere in the record.

near.headline: This point is just outside the 100-foot band as mapped.
near.summary: You are within 50 feet of the band's edge. The band on this map is measured from the stream centerline; the ordinance measures from the ordinary high water mark, top of bank, or channel migration zone, whichever is greater, and adds a 15-foot building setback beyond the buffer. Your property may still be affected.

items.q: Why might I still be affected?
items.a: The regulated buffer starts at the ordinary high water mark (the edge of the channel), top of bank, or channel migration zone, not the centerline shown here, so it extends farther than this map draws. Only a field survey by a qualified professional sets the real line, and the City has published no parcel list.

The draft requires buildings to sit 15 feet back from the buffer edge, up from 5 feet today; the director can reduce it to 5 feet with a critical-areas report. Landscaping, uncovered decks, roof overhangs up to 24 inches, walkways, patios, and rain gardens are allowed in that setback; buildings are not.

outside.headline: This point is outside the proposed 100-foot band as mapped.
outside.summary: Based on the City's mapped creeks, this location is not inside the band. Wetlands, floodplains, piped or unmapped drainages, and the high-water-mark measurement can still bring critical-areas rules into play.

items.a: The City's own consultant (Facet, July 2026, in the Council packet) says the buffer area nearly triples, from 269 to 757 acres (2.1% to 5.8% of the city), on 43.2 stream miles. Our count on the City's own GIS layers shows about 1,490 parcels inside city limits touching the band on mapped creeks, up from about 980 at today's 35 feet. The City must plan for 2,348 new homes by 2046, state middle-housing, ADU and lot-split laws exclude lots inside critical-area buffers, and no one has counted what the band subtracts.

items.q: Is the County doing this too?
items.a: Walla Walla County published its own minimum riparian buffer GIS layer on Aug 31, 2026 using tiered widths of 35, 50, 75, and 100 feet depending on the stream. The County has not yet posted a draft ordinance or hearing dates. The City's draft uses one width, 100 feet, for every creek, even though it adopts the state's four-type stream classification in its definitions.

items.q: Did the City's own Planning Commission support this?
items.a: No. On Sept 14, 2026, after 13 people testified, the Planning Commission voted 7-0 to recommend that Council direct staff to revise the draft to fit the City's infill goals using 'available science matching local conditions.' The draft posted Oct 9 is unchanged: 100 feet on every creek.

outside_city.headline: This address is outside Walla Walla city limits.
outside_city.summary: The City's proposed ordinance applies inside city limits, and the City's stream map stops at the boundary, so this map cannot tell you about this property. In the unincorporated growth area, Walla Walla County's critical-areas rules apply; addresses inside the City of College Place fall under College Place's own code; the County's own August 2026 buffer layer uses tiered widths of 35, 50, 75 and 100 feet, and the County's periodic update is due Dec 31, 2026.

items.q: Why does the map show no creek near me?
items.a: The City's layer only maps streams inside city limits. Reser Creek and the upper reaches of Russell, Caldwell and Yellowhawk creeks are outside the boundary and are not drawn here.

items.q: Will the County do the same thing?
items.a: The County has not published a draft yet. Its August 2026 buffer map is tiered rather than one width. Watch for its hearing dates this fall.

county.headline: This address is outside city limits. The County's working buffer is shown.
county.summary:
The City's ordinance applies only inside city limits. Walla Walla County published its own working riparian buffer layer in August 2026 with tiered widths of 35, 50, 75 and 100 feet; the County has not yet published a draft ordinance or hearing dates (its periodic update is due Dec 31, 2026). Addresses inside College Place fall under College Place's own code.

The City's proposed ordinance applies inside city limits, and the City's stream map stops at the boundary, so this map cannot tell you about this property. In the unincorporated growth area, Walla Walla County's critical-areas rules apply; addresses inside the City of College Place fall under College Place's own code; the County's own August 2026 buffer layer uses tiered widths of 35, 50, 75 and 100 feet, and the County's periodic update is due Dec 31, 2026.

items.a: It is the County's working GIS layer, not an adopted rule. Treat it as the best available preview until the County publishes its draft.

items.q: Why is my creek drawn differently here?
items.a: Inside city limits the map uses the City's layer; outside it uses the County's. They are different datasets with different rules.

college_place.headline: This address is inside the City of College Place.
college_place.summary: College Place has its own critical-areas code and its own stream buffers; the City of Walla Walla's proposed ordinance does not apply here. We found no public College Place buffer layer to draw, so only the city boundary is shown. Check with College Place Planning (509-525-0510) for the rules on your lot.

items.q: Why is nothing drawn on my lot?
items.a: College Place publishes no public GIS buffer layer. The County-mapped creek lines are shown for orientation only; the County's working buffer does not apply inside College Place.

items.q: Is College Place updating its code too?
items.a: Every Growth Management Act city in the county is on the same Dec 31, 2026 periodic-update deadline, but we have not found a College Place draft. Ask College Place Planning.

millcreek.a: Mill Creek is regulated under the City's Shoreline Master Program, not the proposed Critical Areas Ordinance. The SMP sets a 35-foot buffer along the flood channel (Gose St to the Bennington Lake diversion) and shoreline jurisdiction extends 200 feet; the 100-foot creek buffer in the draft does not apply here.

limits.title: Inside the proposed buffer: what it would limit on this lot
limits.near_lead: If the measured line puts you inside, these limits apply.

items.text: No new structures inside the band: house additions toward the creek, a shop, shed, ADU or patio would have to sit outside it.
Buildable area shrinks to what lies outside 100 ft plus the 15-ft building setback beyond the band edge.
Subdividing must lay lots out around the band and setback, and state lot-split, ADU and middle-housing laws exclude lots inside critical-area buffers.
Rebuilding after fire or damage requires a permit application within six months, or the nonconforming right is lost.
Clearing and grading inside the band needs City authorization and a critical-areas report by a qualified professional (valid five years).

ask.headline: Tell the City Council: honor the Planning Commission's 7-0 vote and get the local science before drawing the line.
ask.body: The public hearing is Wednesday, Oct 14, 2026 at 6:30 pm, City Hall, 15 N 3rd Ave (3-minute comments; Zoom ID 845 3179 8905). No vote that night; the adoption vote is scheduled Oct 28. Written comments go to CityClerk@wallawallawa.gov before the hearing so they are in the record. On Sept 14 the City's own Planning Commission voted 7-0 to send this draft back for science matching local conditions; staff's Oct 9 draft still has the flat 100 feet. Ask Council to honor that recommendation: do not adopt Table 6 as written, adopt tiered buffers that match each creek's real condition (as the County's own buffer map does), publish a parcel and housing-capacity analysis first, and protect existing homes in writing.
ask.email_subject: Critical Areas Ordinance (Item 6E): please do not adopt a flat 100-foot buffer on Oct 28
ask.email_body:
Dear Mayor and Councilmembers,

My name is [NAME] and I live at [ADDRESS]. Please include this in the record for the Oct 14 hearing on the Critical Areas Ordinance.

The proposed 100-foot buffer (up from 35 feet, or 50 on Yellowhawk), plus the new 15-foot building setback, [touches my property / affects my neighborhood / affects the city I live in].

On Sept 14 your Planning Commission voted 7-0 to recommend that staff revise this draft using science matching local conditions. The Oct 9 draft still proposes a flat 100 feet on every creek. No state law sets that number; the Department of Fish and Wildlife's own letter on this draft says 'a site evaluation would be best.' Walla Walla County's own August 2026 buffer map is tiered at 35, 50, 75 and 100 feet. The City's consultant says the regulated area goes from 269 to 757 acres, and no parcel count or housing-capacity analysis has been published.

Before the Oct 28 vote, please: (1) do not adopt Table 6 or the 15-foot setback as drafted; (2) honor the 7-0 recommendation and direct staff to return with tiered buffers that reflect each creek's condition and fish use, with a locally scoped science review and written findings under WAC 365-195-915(1)(c); (3) publish a parcel-level and housing-capacity analysis first; and (4) protect existing homes in writing, including repairs, additions and ADUs on the side away from the creek, and rebuilding after fire without losing grandfathered status in six months.

Thank you,
[NAME]
[ADDRESS]

about_data.streams_source: City of Walla Walla GIS, "WW_Streams_Riparian_Buffer" public map service (visible stream centerlines and the City's 100-ft buffer polygon), published Oct 6, 2026; parcels from Walla Walla County GIS Tax_Parcels (data dated Sept 28, 2026)
about_data.method: Buffer bands are offsets from the City's digitized stream centerlines in Washington State Plane South (US feet). The ordinance measures from the ordinary high water mark, top of bank, or channel migration zone, whichever is greater, so the regulated area is larger than drawn. Mill Creek (regulated under the Shoreline Master Program) and piped reaches are not in the City's layer. Parcel counts are ours, computed on the City's layers; the City has published no official parcel count. The City's layer contains every creek named in draft Table 6 except Reser Creek, which lies outside city limits; it also includes Butcher, Lincoln, College, Barber and Kathy creeks, three springs and one short irrigation segment under the draft's 'and others within city limits' language, and it excludes Mill Creek (Shoreline Master Program). Outside city limits the map switches to Walla Walla County's working riparian buffer layer (published Aug 31, 2026; tiered 35, 50, 75 and 100 ft per reach) and County-mapped streams, read live from the County's public service. Mill Creek is drawn from the County layer with the Shoreline Master Program's 35-ft flood-channel buffer; it is excluded from this ordinance.
